opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I think we're at a really exciting but also somewhat delicate moment. If you look at the last two or three years, the progress has been remarkable. Large foundation models, especially vision-language models, have given robots something they never had before: a kind of common-sense understanding of the world. A robot can now look at a cluttered table, understand an instruction like "put the snack in the bowl for the kid," and figure out what that means without anyone programming each step. That was science fiction when I started in this field.

But I always try to separate two things: the demos and the deployments. The demos are getting very impressive. Folding laundry, making coffee, tidying a room. The gap between a great demo and a product that works reliably, every day, in someone's home or factory is still very large. In a demo you might succeed eight out of ten times and that looks amazing on video. In a real application you need something like 99.9% reliability, and you need it in environments you've never seen, with lighting changes, unexpected objects, people walking around. That last stretch of reliability is where most of the hard work is.

So my assessment is roughly this. In structured settings like warehouses, logistics, and some manufacturing, we're already seeing real applications, and that will accelerate quickly. For general-purpose robots in unstructured environments like homes, I think we're still several years away from broad deployment. The core bottleneck isn't really the hardware anymore, and it isn't only the algorithms. It's data. Language models had the whole internet to learn from. Robots don't have an internet of physical interaction data, so we have to collect it, simulate it, or find clever ways to transfer knowledge from video and other sources.

I'm optimistic, though. The trajectory feels similar to where language models were maybe five or six years ago. The ingredients are coming together, and once the data flywheel starts turning, with robots deployed, collecting experience, and improving, I think progress could surprise a lot of people.

r001.rationale: The response says robot demos for specific tasks are impressive while reliable everyday deployment remains a large gap, especially in unstructured environments.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I'd say we're at a genuinely exciting but still early stage, and I try to be honest about both halves of that.

The exciting part is that the way we build robot intelligence has fundamentally changed in the last few years. For most of my career, a robot that could walk, or grasp an object, or navigate a hallway was the result of years of hand-engineering for that one task. Now we have foundation models for robotics, and large language and vision-language models that give robots common sense about the world. A robot today can take an instruction in plain language, look at a scene it has never seen before, and come up with a reasonable plan. That was science fiction when I started working on legged locomotion and sim-to-real transfer. Simulation has also matured to the point where we can train a controller on millions of virtual trials and have it work on real hardware on the first try, and that has made humanoids and quadrupeds dramatically more capable.

The sober part is that there is a big gap between an impressive demo and a product that works reliably every day in someone's home or factory. The demo works nine out of ten times. A real application needs to work nine hundred ninety-nine times out of a thousand, with no engineer standing behind it. Dexterous manipulation is still hard. Robots are still fragile in the long tail of situations, the messy kitchen, the slightly different door handle, the lighting that changes. And data is the bottleneck. Language models had the internet to learn from. Robots do not have an internet of physical experience yet, so everyone is racing to build it through teleoperation, simulation, and video.

So where are we actually seeing deployment? Structured environments first. Warehouses, logistics, some manufacturing, and inspection tasks where the variability is bounded and the economics clearly work. Quadrupeds are already doing real jobs in industrial sites. Humanoids are being piloted in factories, though I'd call that early pilots rather than scale. General-purpose home robots are further away. I think that is a several-year horizon, not a next-year horizon.

My overall assessment is that the research trajectory is steeper than at any point in the field's history, and the gap between capability and reliability is now an engineering and data problem rather than a question of whether it is possible at all. That is a very different and much better place to be than we were in five years ago.

r001.rationale: The response describes impressive robot demos and deployments in bounded, structured settings, while emphasizing the large reliability gap before robots can work consistently in real homes or factories.

astra-6.text:
I think robotics is at an exciting stage, but we need to distinguish between impressive demonstrations and systems that people can rely on every day. A robot completing a task once is very different from completing it thousands of times, safely and at a reasonable cost.

In structured environments, where the tasks and surroundings are predictable, robots already have practical value. The harder step is moving into environments where things change constantly—where a robot has to handle unfamiliar objects, unexpected obstacles, and people moving around it. Progress in AI is helping, but intelligence is only one part of the problem. Hardware reliability, safety, maintenance, and cost all matter.

So I’m optimistic, but I expect adoption to happen task by task. The key question is: can a robot solve a specific customer’s problem reliably enough to justify using it? That’s the transition we need to make from a compelling demo to a useful product.

r001.rationale: The response says robots already have practical value in predictable, structured settings, while moving to changing real-world environments remains a harder step before reliable everyday use.

sol-6.1.text:
I think robotics has made exciting progress, but there’s still a gap between an impressive demonstration and a system that’s useful every day. A robot might succeed in a carefully prepared setting, while a real application requires it to work reliably when the environment changes or something unexpected happens.

So I would look beyond whether a robot can perform a task once. How often does it succeed? How much human intervention does it need? Is it safe, and does the value it creates justify its cost? Those are the questions that determine whether it can move into practical use.

My view is that we’ll see progress first in applications with clear tasks and relatively controlled environments. More general robots will take longer, but those narrower deployments are valuable: they help us understand what actually needs to improve.

r001.rationale: The response says a robot may succeed in a carefully prepared setting while still falling short of reliable everyday use, and notes that clear, controlled tasks are where progress will come first.
